## The Old Model of Toughness

Toughness is conventionally equated with grit, stoicism, emotional control, perseverance, discipline, and playing through pain. Among 160 elite athletes, “perseverance” ranked first. Typical images include a football player resetting a dislocated shoulder, Craig MacTavish—the last NHL player to play without a helmet when he retired in 1997—or a wounded military hero. This model treats toughness as overcoming adversity through suffering and visible refusal to show weakness.

Bobby Knight represents its authoritarian version. In five decades at three universities, he won more than 900 games, reached five Final Fours, and won three NCAA championships. His undefeated 1976 Indiana team, which defeated Michigan to complete a perfect season, remains unmatched. Knight defined toughness as overcoming obstacles without self-pity, and his teams emphasized disciplined, pressing man-to-man defense. But his methods included humiliating “soft” players with tampons, cursing, degrading displays, a 1991 tirade—“This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground…”—and choking a player at practice. His success does not validate abuse: this version of toughness suppresses weakness and uses fear to establish authority and control.

## Parenting, Coaching, and Callousness

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind classified parenting through **responsiveness**—being attuned and supportive—and **demandingness**—setting maturity expectations, supervising, disciplining, and confronting disobedience. Low demandingness with high responsiveness produces permissive parenting; high demandingness with low responsiveness produces authoritarian parenting. Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment, and “because I said so” rather than trust and unconditional love. In a study of more than 1,000 parents, only 31 percent of authoritarian parents said parents should “love their child unconditionally”; another found that 81 percent of Americans thought parents were too soft on children.

Expectations and punishment are not inherently harmful. Problems arise when demands greatly exceed support. The “just right” model combines high expectations with warmth, understanding, and responsiveness. The same principle applies to coaches, managers, and leaders: society has retained demandingness while forgetting care. In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found insult-laden tirades and youth athletes vomiting after extreme workouts. Parents defended making eleven-year-olds continue until they puked by saying, “The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.” This callous model links toughness to thick skin, machismo, “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” and “There’s no crying in baseball!” Research also consistently finds that women quietly handle pain better than men, challenging toughness-as-male-bravado.

## The Costs of Fake Toughness

Callousness confuses pushing through discomfort with ignoring genuine danger. On May 29, 2018, nineteen-year-old University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair began cramping and bending over during the seventh of ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers reportedly yelled to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” It took 34 minutes to remove him after he complained of cramps, another 28 minutes to call 911, and one hour and 28 minutes from his final sprint to the ambulance. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke.

Extreme “toughening” workouts can also cause rhabdomyolysis, in which damaged muscle products enter the bloodstream and overwhelm the kidneys. Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described conditioning intended to “make them suffer,” sometimes to toughen players or “weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.” Authoritarian approaches produce lower independence, more aggression, substance abuse, and risky behavior; in sport they are linked to lower grit, emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In a study of more than 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was associated with substantially more child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, people raised authoritatively adapted worse than those raised nurturingly. Fear creates apparent discipline without independent self-regulation; when punishment or the coach disappears, the behavior often does too.

## Real Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action.” It means maintaining a clear head amid anxiety, fear, pain, uncertainty, or fatigue so that one can choose effectively—not automatically bulldoze forward. Sometimes the right response is to go through discomfort, sometimes around it, under it, or to wait. Toughness requires flexibility and many tools, not one hammer.

Pete Carroll illustrates this model. After losing his NFL head-coaching job in the 1990s, he stopped imitating others and developed an approach that lets players be themselves, “the way they see the world.” He supports meditation and yoga and may replace a heated meeting with ring toss. A star player said, “He’s never negative, doesn’t scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive.” Carroll nevertheless won both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl and uses “always compete” practices. His aim is to build confidence in preparation and capability: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do…” His model replaces control with autonomy, rigid persistence with adaptability, fear with inner drive, and insecurity with quiet confidence.

Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni (“We keep it positive here”) provide comparable examples. Ken Reed summarized the evidence: “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach.” A 2008 Eastern Washington study of nearly 200 basketball players and coaches found that mental toughness did not arise from “autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive” leadership, but from environments emphasizing “trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

## The Author’s Search

The author’s turning point came during the Don Bowden Mile, a 1,609-meter race commemorating Bowden’s 1957 achievement as the first American to break four minutes. At 900 meters, his neck tightened and breathing became a high-pitched gasp. Breaking the race into pieces and trying to “push through” failed; he stopped, unable to breathe. After a year of scopes, echocardiograms, and treadmill and biking exhaustion tests, Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed **paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)**: the vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. Strong emotions and stress can trigger this hyperresponsive reflex, while panic worsens it.

The author had to abandon pushing until he vomited and learn to relax and steady his breathing, neck, and mind under maximum discomfort. Running became a laboratory for principles applicable to parenting, grief, and leadership. Toughness is attainable, not a special trait reserved for the talented. Its four pillars are **Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; Listen to Your Body; Respond Instead of React; and Transcend Discomfort**. Real toughness is inner strength: accepting reality, treating thoughts and emotions as information, and creating enough space to choose an effective response.

## Hope and Religion

Manson presents apathy—remaining on the couch at 2:00 a.m. because inertia makes getting up harder—as a crisis of hope. An infomercial can seem personally insightful by naming loneliness, isolation, hopelessness, and distance from one’s dreams, although these are universal features of the human condition. Everyone suffers, feels victimized to some degree, and struggles with the inherent guilt of existence; when absorbed in personal pain, people forget its universality and mistake generic descriptions for intimate knowledge.

The Feeling Brain needs hope, so the Thinking Brain may accept an absurd promise as “so batshit crazy that it just might work.” Religion combines faith, values, emotional attachment, rituals, scapegoats, and collective action. Shared values amplify hope through a network effect: social validation hijacks the Thinking Brain and lets the Feeling Brain run wild. Groups create belonging and the perception of self-control, but suggestibility also makes them impulsive and irrational, capable of becoming murderous mobs.

## Six Steps for Building a Religion

### 1. Sell Hope to the Hopeless

In Boston in 2005, Manson encountered the LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM), founded by far-left ideologue Lyndon LaRouche. Students displayed 9/11 images captioned “America Deserved It,” pamphlets depicting Dick Cheney with devil’s horns and “Mass Murderer,” and George W. Bush with a Hitler mustache. The LYM claimed that the international order was corrupt, the Iraq War served Bush’s friends’ financial interests, and terrorism and mass shootings were coordinated government efforts; years later it made equivalent claims about Obama.

Its effective message to disaffected, scared, and angry young men was “It’s not your fault.” The system—not parents, professors, college, or even the government—was supposedly responsible. Overthrowing it would end war, suffering, and injustice. Manson’s argument with one student showed him that he had treated a conflict about values as a dispute about reason and evidence: values change through experience, not argument.

Hope requires three elements: a better future (values), confidence in reaching it (self-control), and a community supporting the effort. Young adulthood is especially vulnerable because people must choose identities among overwhelming options, manage themselves without constant authority, and find groups that confirm who they are. LaRouche supplied an explanation for disaffection, a supposed method for changing the world, and a community in which followers fit; therefore, he supplied hope.

People are most impressionable when life is worst, because collapse makes previous values seem inadequate and opens space for replacements. Someone who loses spiritual faith may seek a worldly God; someone who loses family may surrender to race, creed, or nation; someone who loses faith in government may embrace extremism. This helps explain missionary efforts among poor and destitute populations and figures such as Jim Jones, Jesus Christ, and Buddha addressing the poor and downtrodden against corrupt elites. Social media accelerates recruitment through algorithms rewarding extreme posts, but anger alone is insufficient: followers need a coherent vision and the sense that they are joining the winning side of history.

### 2. Choose Your Faith

Faith is unavoidable because evidence and science concern past experience, while hope concerns the future. People act on faith that money, credit, education, happiness, love, health, work, and life matter. Even a nihilist has faith that nothing is more important than anything else: “it’s all faith.” The Feeling Brain’s highest value becomes the **God Value**, the lens through which every other value is interpreted. If it is money, family, respect, conflict, and anxiety are understood through money; if it is love, conflict and separation become especially threatening. Jesus Christ, Muhammad, or the Buddha may function as God Values. Narcissists place faith in their own superiority; codependent people make another person their personal God, organizing life around pleasing or saving that individual.

Evidence cannot verify values, which are subjective and belong to the Feeling Brain. If a meteorite killed half a town, a traditional believer might see punishment for sinners, an atheist evidence against God, a hedonist a reason to party, and a capitalist an investment opportunity in meteorite defense. Evidence normally serves the God Value; the exception is when evidence itself becomes the God Value—the religion of evidence, “science,” which Manson calls arguably humanity’s best achievement.

Manson distinguishes three religions. **Spiritual religions** locate hope in supernatural realities and a better future beyond this life: Christianity, Islam, Judaism, animism, and Greek mythology. **Ideological religions** locate salvation in the natural world and collective faith in systems such as capitalism, communism, environmentalism, liberalism, fascism, and libertarianism. **Interpersonal religions** locate hope in other people, including romantic love, children, sports heroes, political leaders, and celebrities.

Spiritual religions are high-risk/high-reward: difficult to establish but durable because supernatural claims cannot be disproved, and powerful because they can make people willing to die for unverifiable beliefs. They arose partly because, for most of history, “99 percent of the population had no hope of material or physical improvement”; plagues, wars, slavery, and persistent misery made an afterlife necessary to preserve sanity and social order. Ideologies are easier to form but compete with one another and often last only years or decades. Though testable in principle, their complexity and dependence on widespread agreement leave them faith-based. Money, citizenship, and many ethnic categories are socially constructed beliefs. Humans generalize limited evidence across vast populations, so racism and sexism persist through ignorance as well as malice—and still offer adherents hope.

Interpersonal religions make arbitrary systems emotionally meaningful. Sports turn white lines, a green field, and a piece of leather into objects of devotion; Ted Williams becomes an American hero while other athletes are demonized. Politics similarly depends on faith in invented systems and elevates leaders into idols. Fandom around Will Smith, Katy Perry, or Elon Musk offers hope through anticipated films, songs, or inventions. Families are “mini-churches,” and romantic love can become quasi-spiritual. Modern civilization has replaced many intimate tribes with nationalist and internationalist ideologies, making large-scale emotional attachment easier to build.

### 3. Preemptively Invalidate Criticism

A religion protects itself through an us-versus-them dichotomy in which criticism proves that the critic is an enemy: “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists”; “Anyone who criticizes feminism is sexist”; “Anyone who criticizes capitalism is a Communist”; “Anyone who criticizes the president is a traitor”; and anyone who prefers Kobe Bryant to Michael Jordan supposedly understands nothing about basketball. These formulas stop discussion before followers question their beliefs and create a common enemy.

Followers must be told that some people “get it” and will save the world while others will destroy it. Nonbelievers are demonized, and fear and conspiracy theories intensify commitment: vaccines supposedly cause autism because medical companies seek to destroy families; pro-choicers become Satan’s soldiers; climate change becomes a Chinese plot to weaken the United States. Whether justified or not, scapegoats redirect pain, sustain hope, and unite the group.

### 4. Ritual Sacrifice

Manson says he became atheist at twelve partly because of dress clothes, questioned Sunday clothing and biblical logic, wore Nine Inch Nails T-shirts to Sunday school, read Nietzsche, and eventually accepted perfect confirmation marks in exchange for stopping public questions. He later understood that dressing up signals respect for the community and marks one as “us.” Robes similarly signal status and importance at weddings, graduations, funerals, court hearings, baptisms, and sermons.

Rituals make values tangible. Values cannot be adopted through thought alone; they must be lived and experienced. Repeatable, identifiable actions modify or reinforce the Feeling Brain’s value hierarchy. Their longevity connects people to the past, while symbolism connects actions to narratives: communion’s bread and wine represent Christ’s body and sacrifice; parades, flags, and fireworks signify a country’s founding or wars; couples’ gifts, anniversaries, and private habits reaffirm their interpersonal religion.

Rituals often involve sacrifice because consciousness produces guilt. Keeping an ownerless $100 wallet creates guilt because something good happened without being deserved. More fundamentally, existence itself feels undeserved: one did nothing to earn life and cannot explain why it began. Ancient religions sacrificed humans to repay this debt, later replacing literal sacrifice with symbolic sacrifice, such as Jesus’s life for humanity’s salvation. Prayer alleviates guilt through gratitude and confession. Ideological religions redirect guilt into national service or sacrifice for society; interpersonal religions use marriage vows, rings, gifts, anniversaries, and daily acts such as “wiping the piss off the floor when I miss the toilet” to make people feel worthy of love.

### 5. Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell

The more absolute a religion’s promises—salvation, enlightenment, perfect happiness, or world peace—the more followers fail, blame themselves, feel guilty, and obey more intensely. Pyramid schemes show the cycle: someone buys unwanted products, fails to recruit others, sees the person at the top with a Ferrari, and concludes that personal inadequacy—not fraud—is the problem. Seminars use music, chants, and slogans such as “Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!” to intensify commitment without teaching how to sell anything.

The same pattern appears in fitness, diets, political activism, self-help, and financial planning: the more one participates, the more one is told is necessary, yet the promised satisfaction never arrives. Human pain is a game of Whac-A-Mole: reducing one pain brings another. Pain may change shape or become less catastrophic, but it never disappears. Leaders stay in business by blaming followers or a nebulous “them” rather than admitting that human nature generates pain.

No religion, country, or political philosophy can permanently solve suffering. Perfect fairness, safety, freedom, equality, or absolution is impossible because every solution involves trade-offs and someone remains disadvantaged. There are “no solutions, only stopgap measures, only incremental improvements, only slightly better forms of fuckedness than others.” The appropriate response is to stop fleeing this condition and accept it.

### 6. Prophet for Profit

Once followers surrender money, labor, votes, or lives, a leader can promise sex slaves, land, office, or prestige by inventing scripture and defining righteousness. The prophet decides what is ethical and who is righteous while trampling other people’s hopes.

Nobody stands outside religion. Everyone adopts values, participates in rituals, makes sacrifices, draws us-versus-them boundaries, and relies on faith to survive. Shared value hierarchies attract, organize, and propel human systems in Darwinian competition. Religions compete for resources; those whose hierarchies use labor and capital efficiently spread, stabilize, and become cultural foundations.

Success eventually corrupts the winning religion. Its God Value shifts from the principles that created it toward preserving its own power and gains—organizational narcissism. This turns “Jesus to the Crusades,” “Marxism to the gulags,” and “a wedding chapel to divorce court.” Decay invites newer, reactionary religions to replace it. Success is precarious because it creates more to lose and because fulfilled hopes reveal unforeseen flaws and sacrifices. The governing paradox is that “the only thing that can ever truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.”

A religion protects itself through an us-versus-them dichotomy in which criticism proves that the critic is an enemy: “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists”; “Anyone who criticizes feminism is sexist”; “Anyone who criticizes capitalism is a Communist”; “Anyone who criticizes the president is a traitor”; and anyone who prefers Kobe Bryant to Michael Jordan supposedly understands nothing about basketball. Such formulas prevent discussion before followers question their beliefs and provide a common enemy.

Followers must be told that some people “get it” and will save the world while others will destroy it. Nonbelievers must be demonized, and fear and conspiracy theories intensify commitment: vaccines supposedly cause autism because medical companies seek to destroy families; pro-choicers become Satan’s soldiers; climate change becomes a Chinese plot to weaken the United States. Common enemies redirect pain, sustain hope, and unite the group, whether or not the scapegoat is justified.

### Step Four: Ritual Sacrifice

Manson’s childhood skepticism toward Christianity—he became atheist at twelve partly because of dress clothes, questioned Sunday clothing and biblical logic, wore Nine Inch Nails T-shirts to Sunday school, read Nietzsche, and eventually accepted a teacher’s offer of perfect confirmation marks in exchange for stopping public questions—later gave way to an understanding of ritual. Dressing up signals respect for the community and marks one as “us.” Robes similarly signal status and importance at weddings, graduations, funerals, court hearings, baptisms, and sermons.

Rituals make values tangible. Values cannot be adopted by thinking alone; they must be lived and experienced. Repeatable, identifiable actions modify or reinforce the Feeling Brain’s value hierarchy. Their longevity connects people to the past, while symbolism connects actions to narratives: communion’s bread and wine represent Christ’s body and sacrifice; national parades, flags, and fireworks signify a country’s founding or wars; couples’ gifts, anniversaries, and private habits reaffirm their interpersonal religion.

Rituals often involve sacrifice because consciousness produces guilt. Finding and keeping an ownerless $100 wallet creates guilt because something good happened without being deserved. More fundamentally, existence itself feels undeserved: one did nothing to earn life and cannot explain why it began. Ancient religions sacrificed humans to repay this debt, later replacing literal sacrifice with symbolic sacrifice, such as Jesus’s life for humanity’s salvation. Prayer similarly functions as guilt alleviation: gratitude for existence combined with confession. Ideological religions redirect guilt into national service or sacrifice for society; interpersonal religions use marriage vows, rings, gifts, anniversaries, and daily acts such as “wiping the piss off the floor when I miss the toilet” to make people feel worthy of love.

### Step Five: Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell

A religion becomes more controlling as its promises become more absolute. Followers inevitably fail to achieve salvation, enlightenment, perfect happiness, or world peace; they then blame themselves, feel guilty, and obey more intensely. Pyramid schemes demonstrate the cycle: someone buys unwanted products, fails to recruit others, sees the person at the top with a Ferrari, and concludes that personal inadequacy—not fraud—is the problem. Seminars use music, chants, and slogans such as “Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!” to intensify commitment without teaching how to sell anything.

The same pattern appears in fitness, diets, political activism, self-help, financial planning, and other systems promising satisfaction that requires ever more participation. Human pain is a game of Whac-A-Mole: reducing one pain brings another, which may be less catastrophic or differently shaped but never disappears. Leaders remain in business by blaming followers or a nebulous “them” rather than admitting that human nature generates pain.

No religion, country, or political philosophy can permanently solve suffering. Perfect fairness, safety, freedom, equality, or absolution is impossible because every solution requires trade-offs and someone remains disadvantaged. There are “no solutions, only stopgap measures, only incremental improvements, only slightly better forms of fuckedness than others.” The appropriate response is to stop fleeing this condition and accept it.

### Step Six: Prophet for Profit

Once followers surrender money, labor, votes, or even their lives, a religious leader can promise sex slaves, land, office, prestige, or personal paradise by inventing scripture and defining righteousness. Shared value hierarchies attract, organize, and propel human systems in Darwinian competition. Religions compete for resources; those whose hierarchies use labor and capital efficiently spread, stabilize, and become cultural foundations.

Success eventually corrupts the winning religion. Its God Value shifts from the principles that created it toward preserving its own power and gains. This organizational narcissism turns “Jesus to the Crusades,” “Marxism to the gulags,” and “a wedding chapel to divorce court.” The resulting decay invites newer, reactionary religions to replace it. Success is precarious because it creates more to lose and because fulfilled hopes reveal that supposedly perfect dreams contain unforeseen flaws and sacrifices. The chapter ends with its governing paradox: “the only thing that can ever truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.”

## Kant and Maturity

Immanuel Kant lived with extraordinary regularity: for forty years he rose at five, wrote for three hours, lectured for four, ate at the same restaurant, walked the same park route, and went to bed at ten. Yet from Königsberg he became one of history’s most influential thinkers. He argued for inherent human dignity, envisioned a global governing body that helped inspire the United Nations, described space and time in ways that influenced Einstein’s relativity, suggested animal rights, reinvented aesthetics, resolved the rationalism–empiricism debate, and transformed moral philosophy. He held that right and wrong transcend emotion and personal advantage, confronting the “Uncomfortable Truth” without relying on hope.

## Child, Adolescent, Adult

Children explore because their Feeling Brains collect information about pleasure and pain. Touching a hot stove teaches that burning hurts; stealing ice cream produces pleasure but also an angry mother and punishment. A deeper value judgment follows: ice cream is better than being burned. As experience becomes too vast to explore directly, children develop abstract rules: flames are dangerous, stealing dessert is bad, and honesty and sharing have consequences. Adolescents can use if/then reasoning, weigh trade-offs, and negotiate personal desires with social rules.

This is cognitive progress, but adolescent values remain transactional. The adolescent does homework to protect the future, calls her mother to avoid being yelled at, obeys a boss for money, or acts nice to avoid conflict. Everything is a means to pleasure or a way to minimize pain: a more sophisticated child planning several moves ahead, but not yet standing for anything outside herself.

Practical competence—job interviews, finances, cleaning, and not being an asshole—prevents childish dysfunction but does not itself constitute adulthood. These actions are usually means to superficial ends. The most important goods are nontransactional: bargaining for love, companionship, respect, trust, or happiness undermines them. If someone must be convinced to love or respect you, the result is not genuine love or respect. Self-help can likewise become “Show me the rules of the game, and I’ll play it,” even though treating happiness as rule-following may prevent it.

Adulthood means doing what is right because it is right, even when it hurts. An adolescent claims to value honesty because it produces good results, then tells white lies or becomes passive-aggressive when truth is costly. An adult treats honesty as inherently valuable—an end rather than a means. An adolescent treats love as an exchange; an adult loves and gives without requiring a return. Maturity concerns intention, not age or outward behavior: the child avoids stealing ice cream because it feels good, the adolescent to prevent punishment, and the adult because stealing is wrong even if she could get away with it.

## Why Development Stalls

Children transcend pleasure-and-pain values by pursuing them and experiencing their failure. Good parenting supplies predictable consequences: punishment for stealing ice cream and reward for sitting quietly in a restaurant teach that the world does not cater to immediate impulses. Without this lesson, the adult is socially punished for selfishness and disregard of rules. Abuse creates the opposite problem: punishment is random, excessive, or absent, so behavior produces no reliable lesson or higher value. The child develops coping mechanisms instead of self-control. This helps explain why abused and coddled children can develop similar adult problems: both may remain trapped in a childhood value system.

Advancing to adolescence requires trust that behavior produces predictable outcomes; the same applies socially. Without trustworthy institutions or leaders, stable rules and roles cannot develop, and behavior reverts toward selfishness. Trauma and neglect can also trap people at the adolescent level. Someone bullied in youth may assume affection and respect are never unconditional, so relationships become performances governed by clothing, speech, and practiced behavior. Some become charming manipulators who conclude that life is one large high-school gymnasium in which people must dominate others before being dominated.

The alternative is to demonstrate unconditionality: trust an adolescent to teach trust, respect him to teach respect, and love him without forcing a return. Parents and teachers often fail because they remain transactional, bargaining love for sex, loyalty for affection, or respect for obedience; the child then reproduces the model across generations. Acting unconditionally requires faith—loving without assurance of being loved, trusting despite possible harm, and choosing virtue despite the possibility that it will not work out. It requires abandoning the expectation that life will become more pleasant and acting rightly anyway.

## Religion and the Formula of Humanity

The world’s great religions direct people toward unconditional values: Jesus Christ’s unconditional forgiveness, the Buddha’s Noble Eightfold Path, and Muhammad’s perfect justice. In pure form, they use hope to pull people toward adult virtues, but human institutions are eventually corrupted by transactional adolescents and narcissistic children. Enlightenment thinkers replaced spirituality with “ideological religions” pursuing measurable goals—greater happiness, less suffering, liberty, compassion, empathy, and equality. These can also become destructive: bargaining for happiness destroys it, enforcing freedom can negate it, and trying to create equality can undermine equality.

The unresolved issue is conditionality. Whatever becomes a person’s “God Value”—a supernatural being, abstract principle, or bottomless desire—may eventually justify sacrificing human life to approach it. Kant sought value without hope. He argued that consciousness is the universe’s uniquely scarce feature: through reason and will, conscious beings can improve the world, create values and systems, direct their fate, and generate increasing complexity. In a thousand years, humanity moved from “twiddling sticks in a small cave” to designing digital realms connecting billions; in another thousand, it might reshape planets and space/time. Thus the supreme value is what conceives value itself: the only true meaning is the ability to form meaning, and the only importance is what decides importance.

Kant’s fundamental duty is preserving and developing consciousness in ourselves and others. He called this the “Formula of Humanity”: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.” It moves people from adolescent bargaining to adult virtue. Hope is transactional—a present action exchanged for an imagined pleasant future—whereas unconditional action respects humanity without requiring a payoff.

The distinction between means and ends clarifies morality. If the narrator wants a Chipotle double-meat burrito, driving, buying gas, and paying are means, and the burrito is the end. If he wants the burrito only to make his wife happy, it becomes a means; if he wants her happiness only to get sex, he treats his wife merely as a means. Lying misdirects another person’s conscious behavior for one’s own end; cheating violates other rational beings’ expectations for personal advantage; violence uses someone as a means to a political or personal objective.

The formula also explains virtue. Honesty is intrinsically good because it does not treat people merely as tools. Courage matters because refusing to act can make oneself or others a means to quiet one’s fear. Humility matters because blind certainty turns others into instruments of one’s ends. The principle requires no future utopia, supernatural faith, or imposed system: conscious will must simply be respected and protected in each moment.

This applies inwardly. Pursuing pleasure as life’s sole goal treats oneself as a means to pleasurable ends. Self-improvement is therefore cultivation of self-respect, not merely happiness: lying to oneself, harming oneself, or calling oneself worthless is as ethically wrong as doing those things to others. Honesty with oneself can increase honesty with others, encouraging their maturation in a ripple effect. The world changes not through mass conversion or comprehensive ideology but through each person’s present dignity and conduct.

## The Modern Maturity Crisis

Democracy assumes that ordinary people are selfish and delusional, so it builds interlocking systems preventing any person or group from completely “hos[ing]” everyone else. Free speech, freedom of the press, privacy, and a fair trial institutionalize the Formula of Humanity by protecting individual dignity. Democracy works partly because it admits that power attracts corrupt, childish people and designs constraints around that fact.

The system is threatened when a group decides its values outrank democracy and replaces democratic principles with a less virtuous political religion. Extremists are childish in Kantian terms: they refuse negotiation, recognize no interests outside their own, cannot appeal to a higher principle, and often seek an authoritarian parent to make everything “all right.” Right-wing extremists may invoke “freedom” while demanding freedom from values that do not fit their own, thereby limiting others’ freedom. Left-wing extremists may invoke “equality” while trying to eliminate all pain, inferiority, or moral adversity, even when this causes pain to others.

The rise of extremism has many complicated, overlapping causes, but the chapter proposes that cultural maturity is deteriorating. The rich world faces less a crisis of material wealth than a crisis of character, virtue, and means and ends. The fundamental political conflict is increasingly not right versus left, communism versus capitalism, or freedom versus equality, but immature, impulsive values on both sides versus the compromising adolescent/adult values capable of respecting principles, limits, and human beings as ends rather than merely as means.

## Meaning, Categories, and Hard Edges

A trusted external system must be more reliable than memory, freeing attention for broader horizons. Organization means that an item’s location matches its meaning: reference belongs with reference, and a call reminder with calls. Clarification comes first; the structure then evolves as “in” is processed and tested. Core distinctions remain stable, although the best arrangement may change with work and life.

The seven categories are: Projects; project support material; calendar actions and information; Next Actions; Waiting For; reference; and Someday/Maybe. Each represents a different agreement about what should remind you, when, and how. They must remain visually, physically, and psychologically distinct. Mixing reference with reading material makes a pile psychologically disappear; placing day-specific actions on Next Actions undermines trust in the calendar; leaving inactive projects on Projects weakens its action-generating focus; and mixing Waiting For with personal actions causes repeated, unproductive thinking.

Once items are clarified, lists and folders are sufficient. Lists—paper pages, folders, or software inventories—track projects, Someday/Maybes, and actions; folders hold reference and project support. Lists fail mainly because entries are unclear or incomplete, not because the method is too simple. They are inventories, not priority rankings: priorities can be chosen intuitively by reviewing the complete inventory against changing conditions.

## Action Reminders

Processing “in” may produce twenty to sixty or seventy or more pending actions, plus delegated items, calendar actions, and Someday/Maybes. Sort reminders by the context that makes action possible.

The calendar is for actions that must occur on a particular day or time: time-specific (“10:00–11:00 meet with Jim”) or day-specific (“Call Rachel Tuesday to see if she got the proposal”). It should show only the day’s “hard landscape.” Do not place an aspirational task on next Monday if it may be moved, because that destroys calendar trust. Most actions belong in “as soon as possible.” If calling to make a medical-checkup appointment takes two minutes or less, do it immediately; calendar the appointment that results.

As-soon-as-possible actions are best grouped by tool, location, or situation: Calls, At Computer, Errands, At Office, At Home, Anywhere, Agendas, and Read/Review. With only twenty-five actions, one list might suffice, including “Buy nails,” “Talk to boss about staff changes,” and “Draft ideas about committee meeting.” With fifty or a hundred, one list forces repeated sorting and obscures brief opportunities. Context lists also conserve energy by supporting consistent modes: phone mode, computer work, or an agenda when the relevant person is present.

Calls should include phone numbers, since lookup may determine whether a call gets made. Allen keeps Online separate from At Computer because flying without Wi-Fi prevents web- or server-dependent actions. Errands might include “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Pick up suit at the tailor,” and “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist”; a “hardware store” item can carry a sublist. GPS reminders may supplement, but not replace, a rigorously reviewed integrated inventory; relying on them alone is “quite overoptimistic.” At Office can include purging a filing cabinet or printing and reviewing a large document; in “Hotel-ing” environments it may mean any company location or separate At Office “A” and “B” lists. At Home might include “Hang new watercolor print,” “Organize travel accessories,” and “Switch closets to winter clothes”; “At Starbucks” is valid when that setting is distinct.

Agendas collect topics for recurring interactions. Separate lists may be useful for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, financial advisers, accountants, computer consultants, and staff, project, board, committee, or parent/teacher meetings; professionals may need three to fifteen agendas, while a contractor’s list can be temporary. Read/Review is for printed material requiring more than two minutes, kept in a defined tray or portable folder. Attorneys and others may need Review/Respond; digital items may go into Review/Watch or Surf Web.

Waiting For tracks deliverables owed by others—such as theater tickets, an office scanner, or a client’s approval—not your own next action. Record both request and agreed due dates so follow-up can be specific: “I placed the order March twentieth” or “You’ve had the proposal now for three weeks.” A workflow can move from calling a vendor for a proposal, to Waiting For, to Read/Review or At Computer when it arrives, then back to Waiting For after sending it to a boss.

Normally extract actions from e-mails, notes, texts, or voice mails and discard or archive the trigger. Exceptions include magazines and articles placed directly in Read/Review, paper bills in “Bills to Pay” or “Financial to Process,” and receipts in a Receipts to Process folder—but only if those containers are reliably reviewed. Sort documents by next action, not document type: a service order needing a call belongs with Calls, one needing computer work with At Computer, and one awaiting information with Waiting For.

E-mail users may use @ACTION and @WAITING FOR folders, prefixed so they sit above reference folders. If the inbox never exceeds one screenful, it may suffice; otherwise move actionable messages out of “in.” Emptying it means deleting, filing, doing two-minute responses, and relocating action and waiting reminders—not completing everything. Review @ACTION like an At Computer list. Dispersed reminders are safe only when every category is reviewed; off-screen digital data can disappear psychologically, which explains why some people trust a paper planner more.

## Project Reminders and Support

A project is any desired outcome requiring more than one action. The Projects list is a comprehensive index of open loops, not a plan, priority ranking, or work list: projects cannot be done, only actions can. Its principal value appears in the Weekly Review, which verifies that every project has a current action and that nothing is slipping. It supports control, reduces subtle tension, links larger commitments to daily activity, and enables renegotiation with bosses, staff, partners, and family.

The broad definition captures “look into getting a dog for our kids” and “find a good tailor.” Hidden projects emerge from calendar and current activities, higher-horizon commitments, and problems, process improvements, or opportunities. “Call Mario re: the fund-raising event” may conceal “Finalize the fund-raiser.” Problems become projects when treated as potentially resolvable, even if resolution is uncertain: “Look into improving Frederick’s relationship with his school,” “Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance,” and “Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner.”

One master list usually works best, but subdivisions are acceptable if all are reviewed: Personal/Professional, Projects—Delegated, Projects—Presentations, sales relationships, or Finance, Sales, and Operations. Personal projects require weekday review too. Subprojects may remain in support material or become separate entries according to dependencies and independent progress. During a move, Allen expanded “Move to Amsterdam” into fifteen projects, including “Set up Dutch bank accounts” and “Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara.”

Project support material contains resources for thinking and action, not reminders. Put the outcome on Projects and actions or Waiting For items on their appropriate lists; consult support files while doing or reviewing an action. “Upgrades—37 Pinkerton Place,” for example, could contain patio, kitchen, and office plans while next actions remain elsewhere. Digital notes, folders such as “Johnson Partnership—Active” and “Johnson Partnership—Archive,” paper folders, and notebooks all work if actions are extracted, notes reviewed, and stale material removed. Digital systems can scatter information across uncoordinated locations and recreate mental tracking; CRMs cannot yet be wholly trusted for subtle, changing commitments.

## Nonactionable Data and Future Options

Reference is a library, not an action reminder. It may occupy one to four physical drawers, many e-mail folders, or extensive digital space; Allen’s restaurant information alone fills hundreds of folders and subfolders. Topics needing more than fifty folders or major documents may deserve a dedicated section or database. Contact managers store phone numbers, e-mails, birthdays, family, and professional data—not reminders, unless an integrated CRM supplies action triggers. Store material according to purpose and access: mobile information on a device, meeting material in a briefcase, office material in files, and rare material in archives or the cloud. There is no perfect reference system; weigh value against capture and maintenance effort.

Someday/Maybe holds possibilities such as “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” and “Get a vacation cottage,” along with trips, books, skills, hobbies, gifts, food, children, music, and movies. It frees imagination without forcing commitment. Allen’s learning to play the flute and sail in the open ocean began there. ## The Junction Boys Myth

In 1954, Texas A&M coach Paul “Bear” Bryant took nearly one hundred players to Junction, Texas, for a ten-day camp intended to “separate the quitters from the keepers.” Heat, drought, and brutal practice drove nearly seventy away: “We went out there in two buses and came back in one.” Although the camp became a toughness blueprint after A&M went 9–0 in 1956, the team first went 1–9, and only eight Junction survivors played on the undefeated team. Its stars—Heisman winner John David Crow, quarterback Jim Wright, and All-American tackle Charlie Krueger—were freshmen who had not attended camp. Improvement also depended on blue-chip recruits, sometimes obtained by bending or breaking recruiting rules. Future NFL players Fred Broussard and Joe Boring and future TOPGUN pilot Foster “Tooter” Teague quit; many survivors stayed because football and school offered few alternatives. Bryant later apologized for mistreating them.

## Sorting Is Not Development

The military was similarly misread. Navy SEAL Hell Week primarily sorted people able to withstand war’s demands; it was not itself a toughness-development method. Extreme stress can produce **dissociation**—amnesia, depersonalization, or derealization—as perception, memory, and action deteriorate. Research found symptoms in 96 percent of soldiers; 65 percent of experienced soldiers had “lost track of what was going on,” and all but two of ninety-four felt they viewed the world “through a fog.”

SERE (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape), created after Korean War POW casualties, supplies the missing sequence: classroom instruction precedes wilderness evasion and simulated detention. Its 652-page Air Force manual covers medicine, camouflage, fire making, “river hydraulics,” and psychological skills for boredom, loneliness, and hopelessness. **Stress inoculation** works when relevant skills are taught first, then practiced under challenging but non-overwhelming conditions. Later programs added goal setting, self-talk, stress management, and resilience; by 2018, the Army was the country’s largest employer of sports psychologists. Comprehensive Soldier Fitness and the 2015 Human Dimension Strategy emphasized emotion regulation, social intelligence, decision making, holistic health, and long-term resilience.

## How Toughness Works

Clear-headed soldiers appraised stress as challenge, used flexible coping, processed internal signals without immediately reacting, and changed physiological state. Toughness is not immunity to discomfort or absence of quitting thoughts; such thoughts are normal. It is navigating discomfort through **Feel → Inner debate → Urge → Decision**. Stress and fatigue shorten this sequence toward escape because the brain seeks closure and reduces uncertainty. Real toughness creates enough space to guide the response toward the appropriate action rather than the quickest one.

At Auschwitz—an area slightly larger than Central Park—more than 1.3 million people were systematically sorted, enslaved, tortured, and murdered over four years. Witold Pilecki, a decorated veteran of the 1918 Polish-Soviet War, helped form the Secret Polish Army after Nazi and Soviet invasions destroyed Poland in 1939. Materially, the present is arguably history’s best period, yet hopelessness is spreading through wealthy, developed societies. ## Marginal Gains and Compounding

In 2003, Dave Brailsford took over British Cycling after nearly a century of mediocrity: since 1908, British riders had won one Olympic gold medal, and no British cyclist had won the Tour de France in 110 years. He pursued “the aggregation of marginal gains”: improve every element of cycling by 1 percent. The team redesigned seats, rubbed alcohol on tires, used heated overshorts and biofeedback sensors, tested fabrics in a wind tunnel, optimized massage gels, taught riders hand-washing, selected pillows and mattresses, and painted its truck white to reveal dust. Within five years, Britain won 60 percent of cycling gold medals at Beijing 2008; in 2012 it set nine Olympic and seven world records. Bradley Wiggins won the 2012 Tour de France, followed by Chris Froome in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017. From 2007 to 2017, British cyclists won 178 world championships and sixty-six Olympic or Paralympic gold medals.

Habits are “the compound interest of self-improvement.” Improving 1 percent daily produces results nearly thirty-seven times better after a year; declining 1 percent daily approaches zero. Small choices may be imperceptible, but repetition makes them decisive: a 3.5-degree change in an airplane’s heading from Los Angeles sends it to Washington, D.C., rather than New York. Outcomes are lagging measures of repeated behavior, so trajectory matters more than present results. Good habits make time an ally; bad habits make it an enemy.

## Delayed Progress

Compounding often produces a “Valley of Disappointment” before a breakthrough. An ice cube remains unmelted from twenty-five through thirty-one degrees, then melts at thirty-two. Cancer may remain undetectable for 80 percent of its development; bamboo builds roots for five years before rising ninety feet in six weeks. Work during the “Plateau of Latent Potential” is stored rather than wasted. As Jacob Riis’s quote in the San Antonio Spurs’ locker room puts it, the hundred-and-first hammer blow splits the stone because of all that came before.

## Systems over Goals

Goals define desired results; systems are the processes producing them. Winners and losers often share goals, as British cyclists did before their system changed. Goals can create only temporary change, defer happiness, and produce a post-achievement “yo-yo” effect. Goals set direction, but systems create progress and sustain improvement. An atomic habit is a small, repeatable practice embedded in a larger system—the building block of compound growth. “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.”
